name: PIR Motion Sensor
tagline: Sees changes in infrared, not movement — it detects a warm body crossing its beams.
terminals: N — neutral (most mains sensors need one)
L' or SL — switched live out to the load
Some designs add a permanent-live loop or an override input
parts: Fresnel lens — splits the view into beams
Pyroelectric element — generates a voltage when IR flux changes
Amplifier and comparator — decides what counts as a detection
Time (TIME) and light level (LUX) adjustment dials
safety: A PIR switches live, so the lamp holder stays live even with the sensor off — isolate at the board, not at the sensor. Detection zones are wider than people expect: a sensor pointed at a road or a neighbour's garden will trigger on passing cars, and one mounted near a heat source such as a boiler flue will false-trigger in still air.

points.label: Housing
points.detail: A UV-stable plastic case rated at least IP44 outdoors. Mount it where the approach runs across the beams rather than straight at the lens — a sensor detects a warm body moving between zones, so someone walking directly towards it is the one case it sees worst.

points.label: Fresnel lens and pyroelectric element
points.detail: The domed lens is a set of facets, each focusing a narrow beam onto the element behind it. Nothing is detected until a heat source moves from one beam to the next, which is why a person standing still inside the detection zone eventually lets the light time out.

points.label: TIME and LUX dials
points.detail: TIME sets how long the load stays on after the last detection — a few seconds to several minutes. LUX sets the ambient light level below which the sensor will work at all, so adjusting it in daylight is what makes a floodlight appear dead at night.

points.label: Swivel bracket
points.detail: A ball joint that lets you aim the lens after the back plate is fixed. Set the angle on the ground and check it again after dark from the approach you actually want covered — the pattern on the box is a cone, not the real footprint on the ground.

points.label: Cable gland and terminals
points.detail: Cable enters from below through a gland so water runs away from the terminals. Inside, L and N feed the electronics permanently and the switched live goes out to the lamp — so the permanent live stays live with the light off, and a sensor cannot be used as the isolator for the fitting it feeds.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of a PIR motion sensor showing the Fresnel lens, pyroelectric element, amplifier board, adjustment trimmers and cable gland

cutawayPoints.label: Fresnel lens
cutawayPoints.detail: The faceted dome is not a cover — it is the optics. Each facet focuses infrared from a different direction onto the element below, so the view is split into beams. Movement is detected as a warm body crossing from one beam to the next, which is why a sensor sees someone walking across its field far better than someone walking straight at it.

cutawayPoints.label: Pyroelectric element
cutawayPoints.detail: A crystal that generates a voltage when the infrared falling on it changes. It responds to change only: a warm body held perfectly still in front of the sensor produces nothing, because the flux is steady. Two sensing areas wired in opposition cancel slow changes like a room warming up, so what is left is movement.

cutawayPoints.label: Amplifier and comparator
cutawayPoints.detail: The element output is tiny, so it is amplified and then compared against a threshold. The comparator decides what counts as a detection and what is noise — a radiator switching on, sunlight moving across a wall, a cat. Getting that decision right is the whole difference between a sensor that works and one the occupants bypass.

cutawayPoints.label: TIME and LUX adjustments
cutawayPoints.detail: Two trimmers: TIME sets how long the output stays on after the last detection, LUX sets how dark it has to be before it will switch at all. Most complaints about a PIR — staying on too long, coming on in daylight — are these two potentiometers, not the sensor.

cutawayPoints.label: Output relay
cutawayPoints.detail: The electronics run at a volt or two; the relay is what switches the lighting circuit. It also means the sensor needs a permanent live and a neutral to work, which is why replacing a plain switch with a PIR often means a new cable rather than a straight swap.

cutawayPoints.label: Cable gland
cutawayPoints.detail: Where the supply and the switched live leave the housing, and the point that decides whether the unit is weatherproof. A gland left loose, or drilled on the underside where water runs down the cable, is how an outdoor sensor fills with water.
